To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Earth system will continue to warm, sea level will continue to rise, and the frequency and magnitude of extreme events will increase.

(1) CMIP5 experiments have provided unprecedented data to advance climate science; and (2) the CMIP5 scientific framework has identified three key scientific gaps for the next phase of the CMIP project (CMIP6), which we have addressed here.

1) the CMIP5 simulations are generally in good agreement with the observations in terms of their global mean temperature, but the agreement is not as good for regional temperatures and the global mean ocean heat content; 2) the CMIP models are in better agreement with the observations for the global mean precipitation, but there is still room for improvement in terms of regional precipitation; and 3) the CMIP6 models are expected to improve on the CMIP5 models for the global mean temperature
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the use of a new generation of coupled climate models for the simulation of the Earth's climate system; (2) the analysis of climate variability, predictablility, and change; and (3) the development and use of new methods to quantify the uncertainty in model projections of climate change.
understanding the role of the ocean and the cryosphere on climate variability and change on a wide range of time scales.
the development of new methods and tools to improve climate model simulations, to better understand climate variability, and to improve climate projections.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

CMIP5 has greatly advanced our understanding of the climate system, but it is also clear that CMIP5 is not the final word in climate model evaluation and that CMIP6 will provide a new and important step in this direction.
the CMIP5 experiments have provided a wealth of information that has advanced our understanding of climate change and its impacts.
CMIP5 has been a great success and CMIP6 will continue this success.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CMIP5 model output is not sufficient to address these three questions.
the CMIP6 framework is now ready for implementation, and that the community is ready to start producing CMIP6 simulations and to use them for science.

we have shown how the Earth system responds to changes in forcing, and have motivated three broad topics that guided the scientific design of the next phase CMIP6: (1) How does the Earth system response to changes in forcing?(2) What are the origins and the consequences of systematic model errors?(3) How can we assess future changes given internal climate variation, predictability, uncertainties in scenarios?
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CMIP community should be aware of the scientific gaps and recommendations that are presented here.

CMIP has demonstrated the importance of coordinated experiments and model output for climate science, and that CMIP6 should continue to do so, with the aim of providing the scientific community with the most comprehensive and consistent model output to address the most pressing science questions.
there is a need for a more systematic approach in CMIP to address the above questions.
